match.reason: The bank point covers global health inequities broadly, with clean water and sanitation as only one of several drivers, so it is broader than the focused new point on safe water and sanitation and its spread of disease.

draft.title: Safe water and sanitation
card: Safe water is water free from germs and harmful chemicals. Sanitation means safe toilets and the safe disposal of human waste.
Without them, germs from faeces can get into drinking water, food and hands. This spreads diseases such as diarrhoea and cholera.
Diarrhoea is a leading cause of death in children under five in poorer countries. It causes a loss of body fluids, and young children are less able to cope with that loss.
Repeated illness also lowers development. Children miss school, and adults miss work. Time spent collecting water is also lost to other activities.
draft.remember: Unsafe water and poor sanitation spread disease, which harms both health and development.

a.q: Why does a lack of toilets in a village increase the spread of diarrhoea?
opts: Faeces can contaminate water, food and hands
Dry air makes germs spread faster between people
People drink too little water to stay healthy
Children eat too much food that is hard to digest
a.why: Without toilets, human waste is not kept apart from water and food, so germs reach people's mouths. Drinking too little water is not the cause. Diarrhoea is spread by germs from contaminated sources.
a.clue: Think about where the germs in human waste end up.

b.q: A school in rural Malawi gets a bore with safe water and new toilets. Absences fall. Which is the best explanation?
opts: Fewer children are ill from water-borne disease
Children now have more free time to play outside
Teachers now offer lessons that are more interesting
Families now earn more money from selling water
b.why: Safe water and toilets cut the spread of germs, so fewer children are sick and miss school. Nothing in the case says family income rose, and the change is linked to health. Better attendance supports development.
b.clue: Which answer links the new facilities to illness?

a.best: Faeces can contaminate water, food and hands

b.best: Fewer children are ill from water-borne disease

The distractors ('Dry air makes germs spread faster', 'Children eat too much food that is hard to digest') are implausible, so the question is too easy for Year 12.

proposal.title: Safe water and sanitation
card: Safe water is water free from germs and harmful chemicals. Sanitation means safe toilets and the safe disposal of human waste.
Without them, germs from faeces can get into drinking water, food and hands. This spreads diseases such as diarrhoea and cholera.

proposal.remember: Unsafe water and poor sanitation spread disease, which harms both health and development.

a.q: A village has no toilets, so people relieve themselves near the stream they drink from. Why does diarrhoea spread?
opts: Germs from faeces reach drinking water, food and hands
Open waste breeds mosquitoes that carry diarrhoea germs
People there drink too little and become dehydrated
Diarrhoea germs pass mainly through coughs and sneezes
a.why: Without toilets, faeces are not kept apart from water and food, so germs reach people's mouths. Dehydration is an effect of diarrhoea, not the way it spreads. Mosquitoes spread other diseases, such as malaria, not diarrhoea.
a.clue: Follow the path from the waste to someone's mouth.

b.q: A school in rural Malawi gets a bore with safe water and new toilets. Absences fall. Which is the best explanation?
opts: Fewer children are ill from water-borne disease
Children drink more water, so they focus better in class
Teachers now offer lessons that are more interesting
Families now earn more money from selling water
b.why: Safe water and toilets cut the spread of germs from faeces, so fewer children are sick and miss school. Drinking more water may help focus, but it does not explain why children stopped staying home. Better attendance supports development.
b.clue: Think about what kept children at home before the change.
